C0.quote: Election of the challenger requires a majority of the votes
C0.note: Borderline. This is a lobbying/electoral-competition model with a two-candidate majority election, studying the strategic behaviour of a candidate under micro-targeting. Coded as strategic aspects of a voting procedure.

C1.quote: The analysis fully characterizes the set of influential MT equilibria.
C1.note: Main results characterise PBE in which the challenger accepts or rejects interest-group offers. SB is added because the challenger's incentives to deviate are central.

C2.2.note: Binary choice between two candidates (challenger vs incumbent), aggregated by majority with ties going to the incumbent.

C2.3.quote: Given implemented policy p, the utility of the group j
C2.3.note: Voters have ideal policies, issue weights alpha and utilities W_j.

C2.4.note: The vote is a separate object, derived from comparing expected utility under posterior beliefs (eq. 2). IDS could also fit because of the sincerity statement; DIST is the first listed.

C3.1.note: Voters vote sincerely given Bayesian beliefs; no strategic voting is analysed.

C5.1.quote: influence simply means an IG’s ability to change the policy outcome
C5.1.note: Results concern changes in policy outcome (influence) and polarisation, not welfare, efficiency or representation. Welfare is mentioned only as future research in the conclusion.

VOT.note: Voters form Bayesian posteriors about which IG got access, but their vote choice is sincere.

CAN.note: The challenger is strategic. The incumbent is passive with a fixed policy.

OTH.note: Interest groups (IGs) make fixed offers to the challenger and endorse her to their members.

C7.2.note: A reason is given for the IGs' fixed behaviour (no lobbying cost). No reason is given for sincere voters.

claims.quote: Our results may offer valuable insights into the real-world elections.
MT can be a decisive factor in close elections
MT can contribute to political polarization by reinforcing existing beliefs

C9.1.note: Claims about real elections and institutions; no welfare or rule-choice claims.

C9.2.note: Needed assumptions are stated: sincere voters, a strategic challenger, the challenger's information, random single-IG access and passive IGs. The 'reinforcing beliefs' mechanism is not modelled, but this is an extrapolation rather than an unstated modelling assumption.
